paras.text: Statutory Interpretation & Legal Research — Audio Lecture

Every other chapter in this track hands you a rule and a case. This chapter hands you the machine that produces those rules. Once you know how a Michigan court actually reads a sentence of a statute, you stop needing someone else to tell you the answer, because you can work it out yourself, the same way a judge does.
Seven ideas, in the order Michigan courts apply them. I will ask you a question after most of them, then go quiet. Answer out loud.
Idea one. Sun Valley, and the four-step framework underneath everything else.

Sun Valley Foods Company versus Ward, Michigan Supreme Court, decided June twenty ninth, nineteen ninety nine. The actual dispute was small, a ten day deadline in a garnishment statute, arguing about whether it governed the filing of an appeal or the posting of a bond. But the Court used that small dispute to state, as cleanly as Michigan law ever states it, the order of operations for reading any statute at all.
Step one. The goal is legislative intent. The Court's own words: the primary task is to discern and give effect to the intent of the Legislature.
Step two. The words of the statute are the best evidence of that intent. Not legislative debate, not a sponsor's press release, not what feels fair. The text, first.

Step three. If the language is unambiguous, enforce it as written. No further judicial construction is required or permitted. A judge cannot look at a clear statute, decide a different result would be nicer, and bend it.
Step four. Only ambiguity opens the door to anything else. Only where the statutory language is ambiguous may a court properly go beyond the words of the statute.

Here is the part that tells you how Michigan courts actually work day to day. Sun Valley resolved its own case using a grammatical tool called the last antecedent rule, which says a modifying word or clause attaches only to the term sitting right before it, not to everything earlier in the sentence. The Court read the statute that way, found no ambiguity, and never had to reach for anything else. No committee report, no sweeping interpretive canon. Grammar did the whole job.

Question. A policy exclusion lists flood, surface water, waves, tidal water, or overflow of a body of water, whether driven by wind or not. A homeowner argues that last phrase modifies only overflow of a body of water, so wind driven rain elsewhere in the list is still covered. What tool decides that argument, and does it wait for a finding of ambiguity first?
Pause for six seconds.

The last antecedent rule decides it, and it does not wait for ambiguity. It is a grammar level reading applied directly to the sentence, the same way Sun Valley applied it, before anyone ever gets to canons or fairness.
Idea two. The canon toolkit, and why each one needs an actual Michigan case behind it.

If the text genuinely does not resolve the question, Michigan courts reach for a known set of tools. I am going to give you four, each with the real case that applies it, because a canon with no Michigan citation attached is just a name you heard somewhere.

In pari materia means statutes on the same subject are read together as one law. Potter versus McLeary, Michigan Supreme Court, two thousand nine, states it this way: a statute must be read in conjunction with other relevant statutes to correctly ascertain legislative intent, and individual words and phrases should be read in the context of the entire legislative scheme. The doctrine goes back further than that. City of Detroit versus Michigan Bell Telephone Company, nineteen sixty five, said all statutes relating to the same subject, or having the same general purpose, should be read in connection with it, as together constituting one law.

Now here is a nuance worth sitting with, because the tidy classroom version of this rule is slightly too simple. The Michigan Supreme Court has said that in pari materia's application is not necessarily conditioned on a finding of ambiguity. That is the one canon in this chapter that does not strictly wait its turn. But do not run too far with that. The same case also holds that a court may read nothing into an unambiguous statute that is not within the manifest intent of the Legislature. So in pari materia can sharpen or confirm what clear text already means. It cannot be used to quietly rewrite it.

Ejusdem generis means of the same kind. When a statute lists specific items and then adds a general catch all phrase, the catch all is limited to things of the same kind as the list. People versus Smith, nineteen seventy five, is the case: a concealed weapons statute listed dagger, dirk, stiletto, then a general catch all, and the Court held the meaning of the general words is ordinarily restricted by the particular designation, so the catch all reached only other stabbing weapons. A thirty inch rifle did not qualify, because a rifle is a different kind of weapon entirely.

Noscitur a sociis means a word is known by its associates. Tyler versus Livonia Public Schools, nineteen ninety nine, states it directly: a word or phrase is known from its associates and is given meaning by its context or setting. This is the narrower, word level cousin of in pari materia. In pari materia reads whole statutes together. Noscitur a sociis reads one word against the specific words sitting right next to it.

Expressio unius est exclusio alterius means the expression of one thing excludes the others. When the Legislature writes a specific list, anything left off that list is presumed left off on purpose. Michigan Gun Owners versus Ann Arbor Public Schools, two thousand eighteen, applied it this way: the expression of one thing suggests the exclusion of all others, quoting an earlier case, People versus Wilson. The underlying statute named specific local units of government, cities, villages, townships, counties, and left school districts off that list. The Court held school districts were not covered by the preemption, precisely because they were not named.

Question. A policy's mold exclusion lists specific triggers: leak, seepage, flood. A carrier wants to deny a different, unlisted cause by analogy to that list. Which canon cuts against the carrier here, and why?
Pause for six seconds.

Expressio unius est exclusio alterius. Naming a specific list implies the drafter meant to leave everything else where it already was. The carrier cannot use a specific list to sweep in something it chose not to name.

One more tool, and it has the highest bar of all. Legislative history, meaning committee reports, sponsor statements, bill analyses. In re Certified Question, two thousand three, holds resort to legislative history of any form is proper only where a genuine ambiguity exists in the statute. If the text is clear, none of that material matters, no matter how interesting it is.
Idea three. The practitioner move. Argue the text first, because Michigan is a textualist state.

Put steps one and two together and the lesson for anyone arguing a Michigan legal question, statute or insurance contract, is the same. Find the actual words that answer your question and argue those first. Only reach for a canon, for extrinsic evidence, or for a fairness argument once you can actually show the text is ambiguous. This is not a style preference. It is what Michigan courts are required to do. The parallel rule on the contract side, covered in an earlier chapter, is Rory versus Continental Insurance Company, which bars a judge from refusing to enforce clear policy language just because the judge thinks it is unreasonable. Sun Valley is the statute side mirror of that same instinct. If you remember one practical lesson from this entire chapter, make it this one: find the sentence, argue the sentence, and treat fairness as your last resort, not your opening move.
Idea four. Contra proferentem builds on this architecture, it does not sit outside it.

An earlier chapter covers Klapp versus United Insurance Group Agency in full: once an insurance term is genuinely ambiguous, a Michigan court looks at extrinsic evidence first, and only after that fails does it apply contra proferentem, construing the ambiguous term against whoever drafted it, as a last resort tie breaker. Notice that this is exactly the same shape as everything in idea two. Text first. Canons and context only once genuinely ambiguous. A tie breaking presumption only at the very end, after everything else has been tried and found wanting. Contra proferentem is the insurance contract twin of the statutory canons, not a separate, unrelated idea.
Idea five. A DIFS bulletin and a statute are not the same weight, and here is exactly how much weight each one carries.

In re Complaint of Rovas against SBC Michigan, two thousand eight, is the controlling word on this. An agency's interpretation of a statute it administers, like a DIFS bulletin interpreting the insurance code, is entitled to respectful consideration. But, and this is the whole point, the agency's interpretation is not binding on the courts, and it cannot conflict with the Legislature's intent. The Court went further: courts may not abdicate to administrative agencies the constitutional responsibility to construe statutes.

Translate that into a claims fight. A position built only on a DIFS bulletin's wording is persuasive. It shows what the regulator currently believes the rule means, and that is genuinely useful for settlement leverage. But it can be out argued by someone who shows the statute's actual text says something else, and DIFS can rewrite or withdraw that bulletin tomorrow with no legislative vote at all. A position built on the statute's own text is much harder to dislodge, because changing a statute requires an actual act of the Legislature.

Here is a clean, already verified example from elsewhere in this track. DIFS Bulletin twenty twenty six dash sixteen dash I N S announces the current fire insurance maximum withholding figure under the statute as twenty five thousand ninety dollars for the year running July first, twenty twenty six through June thirtieth, twenty twenty seven. The bulletin is not independently creating that number by its own authority. It is DIFS doing the statute's own cost of living indexed math and announcing the result. If DIFS got the math wrong, the governing authority is still the statute's formula, not whatever figure the bulletin happened to print.
Question. A carrier's whole claims position rests on a DIFS bulletin, with no statutory text behind it at all. How strong is that position in front of a judge?
Pause for six seconds.
Weaker than it sounds. Respectful consideration, not binding force. The same position, rebuilt on the statute's own text, is far harder to knock down.
Idea six. The research workflow. Benchbook, then statute, then confirm it is still alive.

Here is the order a working lawyer actually uses, not the order a search engine hands you. Start with the relevant Michigan Judicial Institute benchbook on courts dot michigan dot gov. These are public, written for judges, organized exactly the way a judge thinks through a problem, with citations already attached. They orient you fast.
Then pull the actual statutory text yourself, from the Legislature's own website, rather than trusting the benchbook's summary or a law firm blog's paraphrase.

Then confirm the case you are about to rely on is still good law. A holding that was perfectly solid in nineteen seventy six can be half dead by two thousand five, without ever being formally repealed, because a later case narrows or overrules part of it.

Here is the clean worked example, already fully verified elsewhere in this track. Tom Thomas Organization versus Reliance Insurance Company, nineteen seventy six, created a judge made rule tolling, meaning pausing, a fire policy's one year suit deadline from the time the insured gives notice until the insurer formally denies the claim. Almost thirty years later, Rory versus Continental Insurance Company cut part of Tom Thomas away. Its own words: to the degree that Tom Thomas, Camelot, and their progeny abrogate unambiguous contractual terms on the basis of reasonableness determinations, they are overruled. Read that precisely. It kills only the reasonableness piece, where lower courts had been striking contractual deadlines as unfair. The tolling holding itself survives, and it is now written directly into the statute.

So Tom Thomas is simultaneously good law and dead law, depending on exactly which half of it you try to cite. Citing the reasonableness half as though it still stands is citing a corpse. Citing the tolling half is citing a rule that is not only alive, it is now statutory text.
Question. Someone in a brief cites Tom Thomas for the idea that a one year suit deadline is unreasonable and therefore unenforceable. What is wrong, and what is still true about that case?
Pause for seven seconds.
That cites the half Rory overruled. What is still true is the tolling holding: the clock pauses from notice to formal denial, and that rule now lives directly in the statute itself.
Idea seven. Court structure, translated into cost and leverage.

An earlier chapter already verifies the basic map. District court has exclusive civil jurisdiction up to twenty five thousand dollars. Circuit court is the court of general jurisdiction above that line, hearing felonies and everything else not assigned elsewhere, plus appeals from district and probate court. The Court of Appeals takes appeals as of right from circuit court final judgments. The Michigan Supreme Court reviews only by discretionary leave, which it grants or denies as it chooses.

What that structure actually changes, on a real restoration claim, is not just which building you walk into. It is cost and leverage. A clean twenty two thousand dollar water loss belongs in district court: faster docket, simpler procedure, and if it is small enough, a small claims division where, under a separate statute, lawyers generally are not even part of the fight on either side. A ninety thousand dollar fire claim has to go to circuit court, where discovery is heavier and a jury trial is available if either side demands one within twenty eight days of the answer. That is exactly why a carrier sometimes fights hardest on a mid size claim sitting right near that twenty five thousand dollar line. Pushing the fight into circuit court raises the cost of litigating for everyone, and raised cost is leverage against whichever side has less time or money to spend on it. Knowing, before you ever file anything, which court a given dollar amount lands in tells you how expensive that fight is about to get, and for whom.

Let me leave you with the short version of all seven ideas. Sun Valley: text first, intent through text, unambiguous text enforced as written, canons only once genuinely ambiguous. The toolkit: in pari materia reads related statutes together, and is the one canon that does not strictly wait for ambiguity, ejusdem generis limits a general catch all to the kind of thing already listed, noscitur a sociis reads a word by its neighbors, expressio unius treats a specific list as excluding what is left off it, legislative history only on genuine ambiguity. The practitioner move: argue the sentence, not the feeling. Contra proferentem: the same architecture, applied to contracts. A DIFS bulletin: respectful consideration, never binding, can vanish tomorrow with no legislative vote, while the statute underneath it cannot. The research workflow: benchbook, then statute text, then confirm the case is still alive, with Rory cutting Tom Thomas in half as the proof that good law can go dead without ever being repealed. And court structure: the dollar amount decides which court, and which court decides how expensive the fight gets, and for whom.
If any of the seven questions I asked slowed you down, that is exactly where to go back and drill.
